25-031.r: Bromine → halogen that is a fuming red-brown liquid at room temperature; it evaporates easily into a gas of the same colour.

25-032.r: Bromine (Br, atomic no. 35) → the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature; third lightest halogen, deep red fuming liquid.
25-032.t: Don't confuse with iodine: of the halogens in the options, only bromine is a liquid.

25-033.r: Halogen used as analgesic (pain reliever) → bromine; compounds of bromine act on the peripheral and central nervous system.

25-034.r: Selenium (element 34) → non-metal that is NOT a poor conductor; grey selenium is a photoconductive semiconductor, conducting more when it absorbs light.
25-034.t: Sulfur, bromine and phosphorus are the poor conductors; selenium is the odd one out.

25-035.r: Fluorescent tube → low-pressure mercury vapour + argon (sometimes xenon, neon or krypton); pressure inside about 0.3% of atmospheric pressure.

25-036.r: Ordinary tubelight → mercury vapour with an inert gas, argon or neon, at low pressure; book accepts both (c) and (d). Excited mercury gives UV that makes phosphor glow.
25-036.h: Tubelight = Mercury + Argon/Neon; sodium vapour is not used.

25-039.r: Discharge tubes for optical decoration and advertising (neon signs) → neon gas; also used in discharge lamps and fluorescent bulbs.

26-001.r: Antacids → bases (aluminium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium carbonate, magnesium trisilicate, calcium carbonate) that reduce excess stomach acid.

26-002.r: Aqua regia ('royal water') → 3 parts concentrated HCl + 1 part concentrated nitric acid (HNO3); dissolves noble metals gold, platinum, palladium.
26-002.h: 3 : 1 = HCl : HNO3 — 'Regia' dissolves the royal metal, gold.

26-004.r: The pH scale → measures acidity or basicity of a solution; 0–14; at 25°C pH < 7 acidic, 7 neutral (pure water), > 7 basic.

26-005.r: The pH scale is logarithmic: each unit = 10-fold change in H+ ions; pH 3 → 6 means H+ concentration falls 1000 times (10 × 10 × 10).

26-006.r: At 25°C acidic solutions have pH less than 7 and basic solutions more than 7 → both statements (acidic > 7, basic < 7) are wrong.
26-006.t: The statements swap the facts: acid is BELOW 7, base is ABOVE 7.

26-007.r: A pH of 7 (at 25°C) → both pure water and any neutral solution, so 'more than one'; pH more than 7 → basic solution.

26-009.r: Red litmus turns blue → base, pH more than 7 (at 25°C), so none of 7, 1, 5, 6.5 fits; blue litmus turns red → acid.

26-011.r: Dry HCl gas does not change dry litmus → without water no hydronium (H3O+) ions form; litmus changes colour only when H3O+ ions are present.

26-012.r: Acidic solution → pH less than 7 at 25°C (e.g. 6); H+ ions exceed OH– ions. pH 7 neutral, 8 and 9 basic.

26-013.r: By definition pH = –log[H+]; 0.1 N HCl → [H+] = 0.1 = 10⁻¹ mol/L → pH = 1.0.

26-014.r: Sulfuric acid (H2SO4) → 'basic chemical' of industry; used to refine metals and oil, reduce steel corrosion, make fertilizers, and in petrochemicals.

26-015.r: Acid rain → mainly sulfuric acid (H2SO4, about 70-75%) plus nitric acid (HNO3), formed from sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides with cloud water.

26-018.r: Taj Mahal marble turning pale and lustreless → acid rain; SO2 and nitrogen oxides form sulfuric and nitric acid that attack the marble.

26-019.r: Copper sulphate solution is acidic → hydrolysis: CuSO4 + 2H2O → H2SO4 (strong acid) + Cu(OH)2 (weak base).

26-020.r: Lewis acid = lone-pair acceptor (AlCl3, BF3, FeCl3); Lewis base = lone-pair donor → NH3 (nitrogen has one lone pair) is not a Lewis acid.

26-021.r: Dilute sulfuric acid by adding acid to water, never water to acid; water's high specific heat absorbs the heat. A and R true, R explains A.
26-021.t: Water into acid → sudden heat, violent boiling and splashing of acid.

26-022.r: Amphoteric oxides (react with both acids and bases) → Al2O3 and ZnO; also BeO, SnO, PbO, Cr2O3. CuO is basic, not amphoteric.

26-023.r: Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (CO2) gas, e.g. Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2.

26-024.r: Limewater (calcium hydroxide) turns milky with CO2 → white precipitate of calcium carbonate: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O.
26-024.t: Limewater test detects CO2 (carbon dioxide), not CO (carbon monoxide).

26-025.r: Soda water (CO2 dissolved in water under pressure) → acidic, because CO2 + H2O forms carbonic acid (H2CO3).

26-026.r: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) → contains no oxygen, only hydrogen and chlorine; nitric and sulfuric acids contain oxygen.

26-027.r: Ammonia → dissolves quickly in water; solution (ammonium hydroxide) is basic and turns red litmus blue; gives a white flame with hydrogen chloride.

26-028.r: Baking soda = sodium bicarbonate (sodium hydrogen carbonate), NaHCO3; releases CO2 when heated or mixed with acid, so it is a leavening agent.
26-028.t: Don't confuse NaHCO3 (baking soda) with Na2CO3 (washing soda).

26-029.r: Baking soda = sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO3) → used in baking and in soda-acid fire extinguishers; both statements correct.

26-030.r: Bleaching powder → calcium oxychloride; baking soda → sodium bicarbonate; washing powder → sodium carbonate; Plaster of Paris → calcium sulphate hemihydrate (CaSO4·½H2O), not calcium bicarbonate.

26-032.r: Neela thotha (blue vitriol) → copper sulphate, CuSO4·5H2O.

26-033.r: Copper sulphate (blue vitriol, neela thotha) → kills fungi in water tanks; also a fungicide for field crops.

26-035.r: Washing soda → sodium carbonate; caustic soda → sodium hydroxide; neela thotha → copper sulphate; hypo → sodium thiosulphate.

26-036.r: Neela thotha → copper sulphate; Epsom salt → magnesium sulphate; baking soda → sodium bicarbonate; caustic soda → sodium hydroxide.

26-037.r: Baking soda → sodium bicarbonate = sodium hydrogen carbonate; formula NaHCO3.

26-041.r: Washing soda → sodium carbonate, Na2CO3; used as a detergent.
26-041.t: Na2CO3 = washing soda; NaHCO3 = baking soda; NaOH = caustic soda.

26-043.r: Baking soda = NaHCO3 (anhydrous Na2CO3 is washing soda), used as fire extinguisher; bleaching powder made in Hasenclever (or Backmann) plant → statements 2, 3 correct.

26-044.r: Artificial fruit ripening → ethylene; baking soda → sodium bicarbonate; soft drink → carbon dioxide; quartz → used to make sodium silicate.

26-045.r: Quartz crystals in clocks → silicon dioxide (SiO2), a framework of silicon-oxygen tetrahedra with each oxygen shared by two.

26-046.r: Predominant salt in ocean water → sodium chloride (NaCl, common or table salt); obtained by evaporating salt water.

26-047.r: Table salt (NaCl) → neutral salt formed from a strong acid and a strong base.

26-048.r: The book gives no single answer (*): iodized, sea, rock and processed common salt can all be used as table salt (about 100% sodium chloride).

26-049.r: Iodised salt → mainly potassium iodide (KI); sodium iodide and sodium iodate are also used.
26-049.t: Not free iodine: iodine is added as an iodide or iodate salt.

26-050.r: Wrong statement: barium and strontium occur free in nature → these reactive Group 2 metals occur only as compounds. NaCl speeds Plaster of Paris setting; gypsum slows cement setting.

26-051.r: Bleaching powder (calcium oxychloride, CaOCl2) → light yellowish oxidant that releases chlorine with dilute acid; untrue: it is NOT highly soluble in water.

26-053.r: Eno salt in water → bubbles of carbon dioxide (CO2) gas.

26-054.r: Photographic processing → sodium thiosulphate (hypo) is the fixer; it removes silver bromide from the negative plate or film as a soluble compound.
26-054.c: The book calls sodium thiosulphate an oxidising agent; it is actually a reducing agent. In photography it works as a fixer.

26-055.r: Sodium thiosulphate (hypo) → used in photography and as an antichlor (destroys leftover chlorine or hypochlorite after bleaching).

26-056.r: Fixer in photography (hypo solution) → sodium thiosulphate; also used in extracting gold and silver.

26-059.r: Useful compound in photography → silver bromide (light-sensitive); silver nitrate, sulfuric acid and citric acid are not it.

26-060.r: Photographic plate coating → very fine crystals of silver bromide in gelatin (photosensitive emulsion).
26-060.t: Silver bromide, not silver iodide or chloride.

26-061.r: Smart film (PDLC film, switches glass from clear to frosted) → transparent conductive layer of indium tin oxide (ITO) on PET or glass.

26-062.r: Night-glowing (glow-in-the-dark, phosphorescent) pigment → europium-doped strontium aluminate; used in safety signs, emergency exits, glow paints.

26-063.r: Glazing pottery → zinc oxide; silicon dioxide, aluminium oxide, barium oxide and sodium oxide are also used in glazes.

26-064.r: Deep blue colour in glass → cobalt oxide (coloured glass is made by adding colouring ions).

26-065.r: Ionic compounds (e.g. NaCl, KCl) → insoluble in alcohol (low dielectric constant); in solid state they are bad conductors (no free electrons) → only statement 1 correct.

27-001.r: Simulated primitive Earth conditions → order of appearance: methane → hydrogen cyanide → nitrile → amino acid.
27-001.h: Simple gas first, amino acid last: M-H-N-A.

27-002.r: Carbon → fundamental element of all organic and bio-compounds; carbon atoms bond covalently, mostly with hydrogen, oxygen or nitrogen.

27-004.r: Origin of life → carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen (the option set); biologists list six key elements: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur.

27-005.r: Increasing molecular weight → methane < ethane < propane < butane (1, 2, 3, 4 carbon atoms).

27-006.r: Alkene (olefin) → hydrocarbon with a carbon-carbon double bond; first three: ethylene, propylene, butylene.
27-006.t: Don't confuse alkene ('-ene', double bond) with alkane or alkyne.

27-007.r: Melting points, decreasing → acetic acid (16.6°C) > chloroform (–63.5°C) > ethanol (–114.1°C) > methane (–182.5°C).

27-008.r: Cigarette lighter gas → butane, a flammable hydrocarbon; a Natural Gas Liquid (NGL).

27-009.r: Bhopal Gas Tragedy (night of 2-3 December 1984, Union Carbide pesticide plant) → leak of 42 tonnes of methyl isocyanate (MIC).
27-009.t: Not carbon monoxide or sulfur dioxide: MIC is the Bhopal gas.

27-012.r: Printing ink → from methane: methane is used to make carbon black, which makes black printing ink. Methane is found in marshy areas.

27-013.r: Methane-producing field → paddy (rice) fields, a major source of atmospheric methane: about 50 to 100 million tonnes a year.

27-014.r: Correct pairs: electrocardiography → heart disorder; nicotine → tobacco. Wrong: biogas comes from cow-dung, and DDT is an insecticide.

27-015.r: Ethephon (ethrel) → fruit ripening; it releases ethylene when dissolved in water; a substitute for calcium carbide.

27-016.r: Calcium carbide (CaC2) → used for artificial ripening of fruit; it produces acetylene gas, a ripening agent like ethylene.

27-018.r: Fruit ripening → ethylene, a natural plant hormone.

27-019.r: Gas welding → mixture of oxygen and acetylene.

27-021.r: Acetylene (ethyne) → used in welding; gives vinyl chloride for plastics; made from calcium carbide (not silicon carbide) + water → statements 1, 2 correct.

27-022.r: Benzene (6 C, 6 H; hexagonal ring) → 12 sigma bonds (6 C–C + 6 C–H) and 3 pi bonds.

28-001.r: Ethyl alcohol made unfit (poisonous) for drinking → by adding methanol and pyridine.

28-002.r: Hooch (spurious liquor) tragedies causing blindness and death → methyl alcohol (methanol), poisonous in any ratio.
28-002.t: Ethyl alcohol is drinking alcohol; methyl alcohol is the poison.

28-003.r: Wood spirit → methyl alcohol (CH3OH), obtained by destructive distillation of wood.

28-004.r: Fermentation of sugar (glucose and fructose) → ethyl alcohol.

28-005.r: Zymase (in yeast) → glucose to ethanol + CO2. Invertase → sucrose to glucose + fructose; maltase → maltose to glucose; diastase → starch to maltose.
28-005.h: Zymase = last step to alcohol; invertase inverts cane sugar.

28-006.r: Molasses → raw material for alcohol (rum, 45 to 55% alcohol). Brandy → grapes; whisky → barley, corn; beer → barley; cider → apple.

28-007.r: Beer → fermentation of malt from germinated barley grains; ingredients barley, water, hops, yeast. Whisky is also made from fermented barley.

28-008.r: Police breath test (old breathalyzer) → potassium dichromate-sulfuric acid; alcohol turns orange dichromate green (alcohol oxidised to acetic acid).

29-001.r: Natural rubber → polymer of isoprene (monomer). Polymer = many small monomer molecules joined into one big molecule.

29-003.r: Nylon → not a natural polymer (synthetic); wool, silk and leather are natural polymers.

29-005.r: Ghee → not a polymer; starch, protein and cotton are natural polymers.

29-006.r: Natural silk → protein fibre from moth larvae cocoons; nitrogen is its constituent element.

29-007.r: Cellulose and starch → both made of (+)-glucose units; starch has about 10 to 30% amylose and 70 to 90% amylopectin.

29-008.r: Most abundant organic compound → cellulose, a carbohydrate (polysaccharide of β-D-glucose); chief cell-wall material; wood is mostly cellulose, purest natural form cotton.

29-010.r: Non-cellulosic fibre → nylon (also polyesters); rayon, cotton, hemp, jute and linen are made of cellulose.

29-011.r: Incorrect: acrylic is artificial silk → rayon (from wood pulp) is artificial silk; acrylic resembles wool. Correct: cotton absorbs moisture, polycarbonate CDs, Teflon non-stick.
29-011.t: Rayon = artificial silk; acrylic = like wool.

29-012.r: Not a thermoplastic → neoprene (polychloroprene), a synthetic rubber made by polymerising chloroprene; Teflon, polystyrene, polythene are the thermoplastics here.

29-013.r: PVC (polyvinyl chloride) → synthetic, not biodegradable; cellulose, starch and protein are natural, biodegradable polymers.

29-014.r: The book gives no single answer (*): polythene is made by polymerising ethylene, which is not among methane, ethane, propane, butane.

29-016.r: Book's answer: polyethylene is the 'gas' obtained from plastic.
29-016.c: Polyethylene is not a gas; it is the plastic itself, made by polymerising ethylene gas. Learn it as polythene = polymer of ethylene.

29-017.r: Melamine → thermosetting plastic (sets permanently, cannot be remelted); used for floor tiles, kitchenware, laminates, adhesives, fire-retardant materials.

29-018.r: PET (polyethylene terephthalate, polyester thermoplastic) → fibres blend with wool and cotton; bottles recyclable. Not safe for alcohol; incineration emits greenhouse gases → 1, 3 correct.

29-019.r: All three contain plastic: cigarette butts (cellulose acetate filters), eyeglass lenses (plastic polymers), car tyres (part synthetic rubber).

29-020.r: Hydrogels (water-holding polymer networks) → used in controlled drug delivery; not used at present in mobile air-conditioning. Book's answer: 1 only.
29-020.c: UPSC's answer is (a) 1 only, as printed. The book's explanation also calls point 3 (industrial lubricants) correct, which would fit no option; treat that line as a slip.

29-021.r: Bulletproof vests and helmets → Kevlar, a para-aromatic polyamide fibre (poly-paraphenylene terephthalamide); layers of laminated glass are also used.

29-026.r: Bullet-proof windows/glass → polycarbonate with layers of laminated glass; the book also links laminated glass to bulletproof jackets.

29-028.r: Bulletproof materials → Kevlar (polyamide) and Lexan (polycarbonate); Glyptal is a condensation polymer for paints and lacquers.

29-029.r: True: Teflon and Dacron are polymers; neoprene is synthetic rubber; polythene is polyethylene. False: natural rubber is isoprene, not chloroprene.

29-030.r: Non-stick coating on utensils → Teflon = polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a solid fluorocarbon; melting point about 327°C.

29-034.r: Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) → polymer of the monomer tetrafluoroethylene.

29-036.r: Not a polymer → caprolactam (CPL), an organic compound used as raw material for nylon; nylon, Teflon, polystyrene are polymers.

29-037.r: Not synthetic → fibroin, the insoluble natural protein of silk (with sericin), e.g. from Bombyx mori; Lexan, neoprene and Teflon are synthetic.

29-038.r: PHBV → poly(3-hydroxybutyrate-co-3-hydroxyvalerate): biodegradable, non-toxic polyester copolymer made by bacterial fermentation of sugars or lipids.

29-039.r: PFAS (perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances) → widespread in drinking water, food, packaging; strong C–F bond so hardly degrade; bioaccumulate → all 3 correct.

29-040.r: Bisphenol A (BPA) → key component of polycarbonate plastics and epoxy resins; used in food packaging since the 1960s; can leach into food.

29-042.r: Phenol → used to make Bakelite, a thermosetting phenol-formaldehyde resin (condensation of phenol + formaldehyde) developed by Leo Baekeland in 1907.
